title: Types and Styles
description: Still, sparkling and fortified, and the words that describe a wine's style: colour, sweetness, body.
L: Name the three families of wine

Every wine belongs to one of three families. Still wine has no noticeable bubbles and is most of what you drink. Sparkling wine holds dissolved carbon dioxide. Fortified wine has had grape spirit added. Inside each family you'll find white, rosé and red, dry and sweet.

Fermentation always makes carbon dioxide. Let it escape and the wine is still. Ferment in a sealed bottle or tank and the gas dissolves, building up to about 6 atmospheres in Champagne, roughly three times a car tyre. Add grape spirit and the wine rises to 15 to 22% alcohol; if that happens mid-fermentation, the yeast dies and the wine stays sweet.
Trapped CO2 makes bubbles; added spirit makes fortified
Match each family to what defines it.
The family depends on what happens to the gas and whether spirit is added.

When spirit goes in during fermentation, the yeast stops and natural sugar remains. That is how Port stays sweet. When spirit is added after a dry fermentation, the wine stays dry, as with Fino Sherry. Same idea, different moment, opposite results.
Spirit during: sweet. Spirit after: dry.
Not true. If the spirit is added after the yeast has eaten all the sugar, the wine stays dry. Fino Sherry is fortified and bone dry.
Wines are still, sparkling or fortified
Bubbles come from carbon dioxide trapped during fermentation
Fortified wines have added spirit, and timing decides if they are dry or sweet
Describe three broad styles of white wine
Explain how skins are kept out of white wine
Link a white style to climate and winemaking
Three ways a white can taste

White wines fall into three broad styles. Light and crisp, like Muscadet or Pinot Grigio, with high acidity and little aroma. Aromatic, like Riesling or Gewürztraminer, with intense floral or fruity smells. Full and rich, like oaked Chardonnay, with a weighty, creamy texture.

For white wine the grapes are pressed quickly and the juice is fermented without the skins, so it picks up almost no colour or tannin. Fermentation is usually cool, around 12 to 18 degrees Celsius, which keeps fresh fruit aromas. Fermenting or ageing in oak barrels, as many Chardonnays are, adds body and notes of vanilla and toast.
Why does a white wine have almost no tannin?
The juice ferments without the skins
Tannin comes mostly from skins and seeds. White wine juice is separated from them before fermentation, so very little is extracted.

Cool climates keep acidity high and alcohol moderate, giving crisp whites such as Chablis. Warm climates give riper fruit, more alcohol and a rounder feel, as in many Chardonnays from California or Australia. The same grape can land in different styles depending on where it grows and how it's made.
Which of these push a white wine towards a fuller, richer style?
Warmth gives riper fruit and more alcohol, and oak adds texture and flavour. Early picking and cool climates both keep a wine lighter and crisper.
White wines are broadly crisp, aromatic or rich
The juice ferments without skins, so whites have almost no tannin
Cool climates give crisp whites; warmth and oak give richer ones
Describe light, medium and full-bodied reds
Explain where colour and tannin come from
Match a red style to its grape and climate

Light reds, like Beaujolais or many Pinot Noirs, are pale, juicy and low in tannin. Medium reds, like Chianti or a Merlot from Bordeaux, have more grip and flavour. Full reds, like Barossa Shiraz or Napa Cabernet, are deep in colour, high in tannin and often high in alcohol.

The pulp of almost every black grape is pale. Red wine gets its colour by fermenting the juice with the skins for days or weeks. The longer and warmer this contact, the more colour, tannin and flavour come out. Red fermentations run warmer than white, often 25 to 30 degrees Celsius, to help that extraction.
Colour and tannin come from the skins
Red wine takes its colour from the grape ____.
The colour is in the skins. The pulp of nearly all black grapes is pale, which is why a gentle press can make white juice from black grapes.

Grapes with thick, dark skins, such as Cabernet Sauvignon or Syrah, give more colour and tannin than thin-skinned ones like Pinot Noir or Gamay. Warm climates add ripeness and alcohol. So a thick-skinned grape from a hot place usually makes the fullest red.
Thick skin plus heat gives the fullest reds
Which wine is most likely to be light-bodied?
Gamay is thin-skinned and Beaujolais comes from a moderate climate, so the wine is pale and light. Shiraz and Cabernet from warm places are full-bodied.
Reds range from light and juicy to full and tannic
Colour and tannin come from fermenting with the skins
Thick skins and warm climates make the fullest reds
Explain how rosé gets its colour
Describe the three ways to make rosé
Explain why blending red and white is rare

Rosé is made from black grapes whose juice touches the skins only briefly, usually from 2 to 20 hours. That's enough for a little colour and fruit, but very little tannin. Most rosé is dry, like those of Provence, though some, like White Zinfandel, are sweet.
Rosé: black grapes, short skin contact

Direct pressing squeezes black grapes gently, giving the palest rosés. Short maceration leaves the juice on the skins for some hours, then runs it off to ferment like a white. Saignée, French for bleeding, draws juice off a red wine tank early; the rosé is a by-product and the remaining red becomes more concentrated.
Match each rosé method to how it works.
All three methods limit skin contact. Provence is the region most associated with pale, dry rosé.
Mixing red and white wine to make rosé is banned for most European wines. Rosé Champagne is the famous exception, where a little red wine is often blended in.
In saignée, the main goal of the producer is often the red wine, not the rosé.
Yes. Bleeding off some juice leaves a higher ratio of skins to juice in the tank, so the red becomes deeper. The rosé is a useful by-product.
Rosé gets its colour from a short contact with black grape skins
It is made by direct press, short maceration or saignée
Blending red and white is banned for most European rosé, except Champagne
Explain what gives a wine body
Describe any wine by sweetness and body

Sweetness measures residual sugar, the grape sugar left when fermentation stops. Dry wines have so little you can't taste it, usually under 4 g/l. Off-dry wines have a touch. Sweet wines can have over 100 g/l. Fruit aromas are not sweetness: a wine can smell of ripe peach and be completely dry.

Body is how heavy the wine feels in your mouth, like the difference between skimmed milk, whole milk and cream. Alcohol is the biggest contributor, because it is more viscous than water. Sugar, tannin and extract add to it. A 14.5% Chardonnay feels much fuller than an 11% Riesling.
Alcohol is the main source of body
A wine smells of ripe peaches and honey, but there is no sugar on the palate. How would you describe its sweetness?
Sweetness is about sugar you taste, not aromas you smell. Ripe fruit aromas can make a dry wine seem sweet before you sip it.

With two words you can describe almost any wine. Muscadet is dry and light. Oaked Chardonnay is dry and full. Moscato d'Asti is sweet and light. Sauternes is sweet and full. Use the colour, then sweetness, then body, and you have a sketch that anyone can picture.
Which of these make a wine feel fuller-bodied?
Alcohol, sugar and tannin all add weight. Acidity makes a wine feel fresher and lighter, not heavier.
Sweetness is residual sugar; dry wines have almost none
Body is the weight of the wine, driven mostly by alcohol
Colour, sweetness and body sketch any wine
Sort a wine into its family
Explain how colour and style are made
Describe a wine by sweetness and body
Match each wine to its family or style.
Family first, then style. Port and Fino are both fortified, but the spirit goes in at different moments.
What decides whether a black grape gives a white, rosé or red wine?
How long the juice touches the skins
No skin contact gives white juice, a few hours gives rosé, and days or weeks give red.
A dry wine can smell sweet.
Yes. Aromas of ripe fruit or honey can suggest sweetness, but dry is about sugar on the palate, not the nose.
Which are typical of a full-bodied red?
Thick skins and warmth give colour, tannin and alcohol. Low alcohol points to a lighter wine.
The rosé method that bleeds juice from a red tank is called ____.
Saignée means bleeding. It gives a rosé and a more concentrated red.
Wine is still, sparkling or fortified
Skin contact decides white, rosé or red
Sweetness is sugar; body is weight
Climate and grape shape the style within each colour
